questions.q: What does Containment accomplish, as a distinct phase from Eradication and Recovery?
options: It stops the bleeding — limiting an attacker's ability to do further damage or spread right now
It permanently removes the vulnerability that allowed the attack
It restores all affected systems to normal business operation
It writes the final lessons-learned report
questions.explain: Containment is the immediate action that limits further damage or spread, before Eradication or Recovery begin.

options: The actual cause of the incident — such as malware, an unauthorized account, or a vulnerability
The network connection between the affected system and the rest of the business
The written incident response plan
The SIEM correlation rule that generated the alert
questions.explain: Eradication removes the underlying cause so the incident cannot simply resume once things calm down.

questions.q: Why is attempting Eradication before Containment a losing battle?
options: An attacker can still actively reach and reinfect the system being cleaned
Eradication tools only function after a system has already been restored
There is no real risk — order doesn't actually matter
Eradication automatically triggers Containment regardless of sequence
questions.explain: Trying to clean a system an attacker can still reach means the cleanup can simply be undone or reinfected.

questions.q: Why is restoring a system to normal operation before Eradication is finished risky?
options: The actual cause is still present, which can trigger the same incident again, often within hours
Recovery always takes longer than Containment, regardless of circumstances
It violates NIST SP 800-61 licensing terms
It has no real risk as long as the system is rebooted first
questions.explain: Recovery before Eradication means calling a system 'normal' while its root cause is still present, inviting a repeat incident.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what happens after Containment, Eradication, and Recovery are all genuinely complete?
options: The incident moves into Post-Incident Activity, the lessons-learned review
The incident is immediately closed with no further steps
The team starts Detection & Analysis again from scratch
The written incident response plan is deleted
questions.explain: Only once all three phases are truly finished does the incident move into Post-Incident Activity, closing the NIST lifecycle loop.
